
<epigraph>Every map is a letter to someone who has not arrived.
- An invented surveyor</epigraph>{p}

<chapter>CHAPTER I</chapter>

<chapter_sections>The ferry at Low Harbor – A debt of nine crowns – The cartographer hires a boy – Salt on the wind.</chapter_sections>

The ferry came into Low Harbor on the last tide of October, 1871, riding so low that the gulls walked its rail like inspectors. Ada Quill stepped off with a brass theodolite in one hand and a letter of credit in the other, and neither was worth what she had been promised.

The harbormaster was a narrow man named Osric Penn who kept his ledgers in a biscuit tin. He told her the survey office had closed in the spring and that the nine crowns owed to her were owed, in turn, by a man who had drowned. She thanked him. It was, she said, the most complete account of a debt she had ever received.{p}

She took a room above the chandler’s, where the window faced the marsh. Reeds ran out to the horizon and a single heron stood in them, patient as a fence post. By evening she had drawn the room, the stair, and the street as far as the pump, because drawing a place was the only way she knew of arriving in it.

On the third day a boy came to the door and said he could carry things. His name was Tomás and he was eleven, or would be at Candlemas. His mother sold eels from a barrow and called every stranger señora regardless of evidence. Ada hired him for two pence a day and a share of whatever the marsh turned out to contain.{p}

They went out at first light with the chain and the poles. The boy walked ahead, testing the ground with a willow switch, and where the switch sank he said cuidado without turning round. By noon they had fixed forty-six stations and lost one boot. The wind brought salt, and under the salt the smell of something older, as if the sea had left its cellar door open.

That night she inked the first sheet. She wrote Low Harbor in the corner and under it, smaller, the date, and then sat for a long while looking at the white part of the paper, which was most of it.{p}

<chapter>CHAPTER II</chapter>

{section_break}

<chapter_sections>Five days of rain – The drowned man’s map – A disagreement about north – The heron again.</chapter_sections>

It rained for five days. The marsh rose and took back the stations one by one, and Tomás counted them off from the window like a man reading names. On the sixth morning the water stood level with the chandler’s step and a pair of otters were seen in the high street, going about their business.

Osric Penn sent for her at noon. He had found, at the bottom of the biscuit tin, a map made by the drowned man: a single sheet, much folded, showing the marsh as it had been twenty years before. Every channel on it ran the wrong way. Ada turned it round twice and t{p}hen understood that he had drawn north at the bottom, for reasons of his own.

She laid her sheet beside his. Where hers showed water, his showed a road lined with alder and a place called Saint Bride’s Acre, with a small cross to mark a chapel. Nobody in Low Harbor had heard of it. The harbormaster said the dead were entitled to their opinions, and poured the tea.

Three weeks later the water went down. They walked out along the line of the drowned man’s road and found it under a hand’s depth of silt, cobbled, running straight toward nothing. The boy said camino, and then, because she was paying him, road. At the end of it stood the{p} heron, or another like it, on a stone that had once been a step.

She fixed the stone as station forty-seven. It was the first mark on her sheet that she had not made herself, and she inked it in red and drew 𝄞 beside it, a private sign, meaning: here the map begins to answer back.{p}

{p}

<epilogue>AFTERWORD</epilogue>

<note>The sheet was never finished.</note>
